evening.title: Did Ukraine Use A Mothership To Launch Its Sea Drone Attack On Russian Ships in Benghazi?
evening.text:
The uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) that attacked a Russian Navy corvette and a cargo ship on Sunday were launched from a mothership at sea, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) claimed on Monday. The SBU’s comments appear to be the first official confirmation that Ukraine has ever used a vessel to deliver USVs for an attack. Still, its statement doesn’t prove a mothership was actually used, as there is good reason for misdirecting with such a claim, but it certainly seems more probable than not.

The SBU account also conflicts with statements made on Sunday about the origin of the attacks. Libyan officials claimed that the strikes were launched from a base in their country, while there were also claims, later denied, that the USVs sailed from Albania. For years, we have raised the possibility that Ukraine was using motherships to launch USVs, especially in the Black Sea. In the case of the Benghazi attacks, we directly mentioned that the strikes could have originated from a ship as opposed to the shore.

New Details On The Benghazi Sea Drone Attacks

As we reported yesterday, the Project 20380 Steregushchiy class corvette Merkury sank after being struck by USVs while moored at a dock in the port of Benghazi. A cargo ship was also struck by USVs while in the waters outside of Benghazi.

The SBU provided new details on Monday about these attacks.

“The Defense Forces of Ukraine conducted a unique special operation targeting two Russian military assets near the Libyan port of Benghazi,” the SBU reported on its website. “The targets included the sanctioned dry-cargo vessel MV Angara, used to transport Russian military equipment, and the multi-purpose corvette Merkury, which regularly escorted hostile naval convoys—including the MV Angara.”

“Both vessels constituted legitimate military targets for Ukraine, as they directly supported the Russian Federation’s military capabilities,” SBU added. “The operation involved seven Ukrainian-made uncrewed surface vessels (USVs), which were transported to the designated location and launched from a ‘mothership.’ Despite the enemy’s attempts to destroy the Ukrainian drones from the air, sea, and land, the Security Service’s USVs reached their objective, located the targets, and struck them.”

The attack “resulted in the destruction of the Russian multi-purpose corvette Merkury (hull number 734), a Project 20380 vessel. Seeking refuge within the port proved futile. The ship was part of the Russian Navy and assigned to the aggressor state’s Black Sea Fleet; it had entered service in 2023. A multi-role Ka-27 helicopter was also on board the corvette and went down with the ship.”

The second target “was the Russian dry-cargo ship MV Angara (IMO 9179842), which was used to support Russian military logistics—specifically as part of the so-called ‘Syrian’ and ‘Libyan Express’ operations. The Defense Forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea. Such unique special operations undermine the enemy’s logistical capabilities and force Russia to pay the price for its aggression, even at a strategic distance from Ukraine.”

The SBU did not say where the so-called mothership was located or what kind of vessel it was.

In a post on X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky included an SBU video with a sea drone’s view of a massive explosion on the corvette. The sea drone then approaches the Merkury amidships on the port side before the view cuts to a large ball of fire seen from another sea drone. The ship appears to be approached by a third sea drone, but it is unclear what happened because the video cuts away to a distant view of the ship engulfed in flames.

The video also shows a sea drone approaching the Angara, striking it on the port stern. An aerial view then shows the ship in flames.

On Sunday, it was reported that the cargo ship struck was the Ascalon, which looks similar to the Angara.

Now a day after the attacks, Libya has closed off the section of the port where Merkury was sunk by lining up small boats to block the approach from inside the harbor.

After the initial attacks by Ukrainian USVs years ago, Russia placed layers of barriers across its harbor entry points and around its vessels. These fortifications grew more elaborate with time. The Kerch Bridge received similar passive defenses for protection. Today, these sort of measures are more commonplace globally.

The following video shows a Ukrainian USV being stopped by booms placed across Sevastopol harbor in 2023.

The total lack of basic passive force protection measures in Benghazi is something TWZ editor-in-chief Tyler Rogoway highlighted on X. This clearly made Merkury a juicy target for Ukrainian clandestine elements operating in the Mediterranean.

Competing Cclaims

As we mentioned in the opening of this story, yesterday The Associated Press reported that the USVs were “launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya.” The wire service cited an initial investigation into the attack. However, we noted at the time that we could not confirm whether the attacks came from the land or a vessel.

There was also a claim made by the Clash Report that the USVs were instead launched from Albania, which is about 530 miles due north of Benghazi. However, Albanian officials quickly and vociferously denied that.

“We have taken note of reports alleging that the naval drone attack against a Russian corvette originated from Albanian territory. The reports in question are inaccurate and do not reflect the facts,” the Albanian Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs posted Monday on X. “Albania was not involved in this incident, and its territory was neither used nor made available for the launch or facilitation of such an attack. We categorically reject these allegations, which have been presented without verifiable evidence. We call on those responsible for disseminating them to correct the record and to exercise accuracy, due diligence and responsibility when reporting on matters of such sensitivity.”

Despite the discrepancies, one thing is clear. It is nearly impossible for Ukraine to have launched the attacks on Benghazi from its own shores. The Libyan port city is located roughly 1,300 miles from the nearest point where Ukraine could put a USV in the water. The USVs would have had to travel across the Black Sea, through the Bosporus, into the Aegean and down to Benghazi across the central Med. And it’s not like anyone is claiming this is what occurred. Clearly, the drone boats were launched far closer, likely from a ship operating in the Mediterranean, and in an area Ukraine has known to be operating in for years when it comes to clandestine attacks against Russian naval interests.

Based on imagery from the raid, the USV used was a variant of the Sargan 3000. Naval analyst H.I. Sutton was the first to point that out.

In a September story about the first USV attack on another USV, we described the Sargan 3000 as “6.9 meters (about 22.6 feet) long, 2.2 meters (about 7.2 feet) wide, with an operational radius of up to 1,600 km (about 994 miles) and can carry a payload of 450 kg (about 992 pounds). It travels at an estimated speed range of 40-55 knots.”

It is interesting to note that in the SBU video, the USV attacking the cargo ship had at least two tubes on either side of the hull. We don’t know whether they were for weapons or some sort of countermeasure, such as for smoke dispersal.

It is possible that Ukraine is using the mothership claim as cover for its operations inside Libya or elsewhere in the region, which would be far more of a sensitive issue than having a vessel deliver the sea drones possibly from international waters. The reported presence of Ukrainian forces in Libya has been a major political issue between the two rival factions controlling the country.

Libya has been in a state of near-constant civil conflict since a NATO-led intervention enabled rebels to unseat and kill longtime Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

Currently, the internationally recognized Government of National Unity (GNU) rules the northwest while the Libyan National Army (LNA), led by strongman Khalifa Haftar, controls most of eastern Libya. 

Haftar is backed by Russia. On Monday, his government said the attacks violated Libyan sovereignty and called for an international investigation into “reports regarding the presence of Ukrainian personnel, experts, or military units in western Libya,” according to AFP.

“They cited information suggesting Ukrainian forces might be present in ‘areas around Misrata, Zawiya, and other potential locations,’” the outlet reported. “The attacks on Russian ships are believed to have been coordinated by these units. According to local reports, similar special forces are thought to be operating near Tripoli.”

The Push For Motherships To Deliver Sea Drones And Other Uncrewed Vessels

TWZ first brought up the possibility that Ukraine could be using motherships to launch USVs in 2022 as Kyiv was initiating what would become a large-scale campaign using drone boats against Russia’s Black Sea Fleet. As we have frequently noted, many successful Ukrainian USV attacks have been recorded against Black Sea Fleet vessels and facilities, forcing the general evacuation of Russian naval assets from occupied Crimea and to bases like Novorossiysk in Russia proper. These facilities have all come under attack since the force posture shift.

The U.S., China, Iran and other nations have operated elaborate motherships and some are developing even more advanced purpose-built craft as launch platforms for USVs, UUVs, and aerial drones. At the same time, you do not a need a highly specialized mothership to deploy small uncrewed boats. That can be done by anything from a fishing trawler to a small cargo vessel — and those kinds of ships have one big advantage, they can hide in plain sight. By using normal ships to launch attacks like this, they can come via surprise and the launch platform can continue on with its clandestine mission far from its home shores.

As for what Ukraine’s mothership may look like, we don’t know. But if it does indeed exist, it will very likely look like nothing special at all.

evening.title: Inception - possibly a ShinyHunters reboot - claims seven victims in a week
evening.text:
Don't mind the recent arrests. The ShinyHunters extortion gang may still be operating, just under the new name of Inception, according to Okta's threat intelligence group.

ShinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI, resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October. The crims - and their old data leak site - have since gone dark.

“While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said on Monday.

Okta tracks this threat cluster as O-UNC-053 - the “O-UNC” prefix stands for an Okta Uncategorized cluster, and it uses this label before formally attributing the activity to a named threat group.

While Okta hasn't formally confirmed O-UNC-053 to be the same crime crew as ShinyHunters, the identity and access management provider’s researchers note that it does use nearly identical social engineering tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA).

Plus, they note: O-UNC-053 operators change the themes of their phishing domains about every four to six weeks, and they also post claimed victims on ShinyHunters’ data leak site. In November, however, organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 began appearing on a new data leak site branded as Inception and not ShinyHunters.

The first five - Advanced Micro Devices, Cigna Healthcare, Paychex, PepsiCo, and Henry Schein - appeared November 17 on the site, and all were marked “leaked.” Soon after, security maven Dominic Alvieri questioned if Inception was linked to ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” he wrote on social media.

On November 19, AutoZone appeared on the site, with Inception again claiming to have leaked the auto-parts retailer's files. On Saturday, EV technology firm Lucid Group joined the claimed victims.

None of the seven companies have confirmed breaches, and none responded to The Register’s inquiries. We will update this story when we receive more information.

Okta Threat Intelligence “is unable to validate if published data is authentic,” the researchers said in response to our questions.

In the Monday report, the Okta team does note that Inception’s new data leak site listings “included multiple targets for which Okta Threat Intelligence previously observed O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.”

The infrastructure was registered between six and 19 days before Inception listed the companies on its leak site, and this gap “is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” Diallo and Nickels added.

The Com (short for community) is a loosely knit network of online groups whose young members participate in a range of illicit activities including hacking, swatting, digital extortion, real-life shootings, and other physical violence. Many security researchers consider ShinyHunters to be connected to The Com, along with groups such as Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$, with overlapping memberships and shared infrastructure.

“Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation,” the Okta researchers wrote. “We cannot currently make a high confidence assessment as to whether O-UNC-053 is operating the DLS themselves or is partnering with another extortion actor.”

Regardless, members of the group formerly known as ShinyHunters and/or O-UNC-053 are still roaming the internet, looking for new victims, and conducting voice phishing attacks to steal data and then extort victims' companies for exorbitant sums of money. Consider yourself warned - and turn on phishing-resistant MFA.®

evening.title: Amazon scoops up AI accelerator tech to keep chips busy at all times
evening.text:
Amazon has agreed to buy AI optimization technology from an Israeli startup in a bid to speed up its inference operations.

The house of Bezos on Monday announced a deal to purchase proprietary AI acceleration tech from Decart AI, known as the Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), for an undisclosed amount. Amazon also plans to bring Decart’s three founders and their engineering team into the fold.

Decart’s DOS is designed to push AI hardware closer to its maximum performance across different AI models and hardware platforms. The company claims that most AI chips live their lives without reaching their full potential – practically a sin in this age of increased hardware costs and limited availability – and DOS aims to fix that by operating between the model and the chip, optimizing kernels, compilers, and runtimes for the underlying hardware “so every core stays busy.”

DOS is hardware-agnostic, with Decart saying it supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs, and, most critically for our purposes here, AWS Trainium chips.

“More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost,” Peter DeSantis, Amazon SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, and quantum computing, said in the announcement. “That's the pillar Trainium and our AI efforts are built on, and from our earliest work with Decart, we knew they … would help us push it even further.”

Decart doesn’t offer much in the way of details about its proprietary AI-maxxing tech, but claims it can reduce latency, improve throughput, and reduce the costs associated with training and inference runs.

An Amazon spokesperson clarified to The Register that the deal is an asset purchase and not a full company acquisition, with Amazon only acquiring DOS and the tech behind it as well as personnel. As for what may become of Decart after the deal, that’s unclear. Amazon told us to reach out to Decart to learn what may happen to any remaining employees and the company’s other technology, but we didn’t hear back.

Along with offering its optimization stack, Decart has a couple of different AI models: Lucy, a live video model marketed toward advertisers, live streamers, and the like; and Oasis, a world model AI marketed toward companies working on embodied AI applications.

Decart’s non-DOS assets weren’t mentioned in the press release, and per the Amazon spokesperson we talked to, that means they weren’t part of the deal. We can’t imagine that the Decart team is too upset about the potential abandonment of those models, though: While neither company has disclosed a price, Bloomberg claims its sources value the deal at around $7.5 billion.

If Bloomberg's figure is accurate, that would make this deal one of the most expensive in Amazon’s history, right between its $3.9 billion acquisition of One Medical and its $8.5 billion purchase of film studio MGM. ®

evening.title: Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more
evening.text:
“It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want.

But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. I could end up paying more for my TV because of where I am or more for a software subscription because of my age.

Surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history, smart devices, and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price.

evening.title: Bluetooth brakes are broken as researchers find anyone can control them
evening.text:
Imagine something as mission-critical as the brakes on a trailer being vulnerable to unauthorized control. One Australian manufacturer made the interesting choice of building Bluetooth into a trailer brake controller without adequately securing its critical braking functions.

Anyone within Bluetooth range of an unpatched Elecbrakes trailer controller could potentially trigger its brakes or apply more braking force than intended, without needing to authenticate.

The discovery comes courtesy of a pair of security researchers from Element Digital, Patrick Forck and Jeremy McCarthy. Their investigation began earlier this year when Forck was driving down the road and noticed that his physical Elecbrakes In-Car Remote had connected to someone else's trailer without pairing or prompting him.

“It had connected mid-drive, without pairing or a prompt, to a brake controller that wasn’t mine, on a trailer I’d never seen, belonging to a driver who had no idea,” the researchers wrote. That one-off connection triggered a full-scale investigation by the pair.

For those unfamiliar with trailer brake controllers, these devices are commonly used on larger trailers. Australian manufacturer Elecbrakes sells such controllers in Australia and New Zealand. Depending on jurisdiction, trailers over a certain weight are required to have their own braking system, which Elecbrakes manufactures. Elecbrakes offers two versions that are designed to be easier to install than traditional controllers: One that’s mounted in a vehicle, and one that is mounted directly on a trailer. That trailer-mounted unit can receive Bluetooth commands from the Elecbrakes smartphone app or a separate in-car remote.

Given the importance of such control units to road safety, it’s easy to imagine how serious such a vulnerability could be if it proved to be easy to exploit, and boy, did it.

Forck and McCarthy admitted they’re infrastructure security guys, not software devs, so they turned to Claude Code to dissect a decompiled copy of the Elecbrakes app, which Claude was happy to oblige.

“What came back from the analysis was a map of the device’s entire Bluetooth GATT profile: 47 characteristics across four services, commands sent as plain unencrypted byte arrays, no checksums, no sequence numbers,” the researchers noted. To make matters worse, there was no authentication required for critical braking commands, even though other Bluetooth functions required pairing.

Claude then built a web app that ran in Chrome which was able to access the Bluetooth controls for a nearby Elecbrakes system, and they were able to modify practically every aspect of brake control on a unit owned by one of them.

Pairing failed on a few attempts, but not where it mattered: It allowed the connection without issue for actual brake control. They sent a few bytes to the brake control characteristic, and were shocked.

“The electromagnetic hum at the brake drums was immediate and, frankly, a little sickening,” the pair said. “It said yes to four bytes from a total stranger then energised several tonnes’ worth of brakes and reported back that it had done so, pleased with itself.”

Further experiments managed to modify braking strength based on deceleration speed as well, making it so that the trailer acted unpredictably based on the amount of force a driver applied to stop their vehicle.

To say this is worse than a typical internet-connected device bug is to put it mildly - it even earned a trio of CVEs from CISA, with two of them scoring a CVSS of 9.6.

“The attack surface is ‘anyone within Bluetooth range,’ the skill required is ‘can write four bytes,’ and the victim selection is ‘optional,’ ” Forck and McCarthy said. The fact AI was able to get them to that point in just a couple of days is even more concerning, they added.

“This kind of research used to require a fairly rare and specific skill set,” the pair noted. “It now requires curiosity, a device you own, and an AI that can read bytecode faster than any human.”

Luckily, they appear to have been dealing with a relatively responsive company in Elecbrakes - patches have been deployed for both the in-car and trailer-mounted models of their brake controllers. Installation is a manual process, we note, so if you own a controller from the company, be sure to stop and install the update.

Unfortunately, Elecbrakes has a third controller out there that hasn’t been manufactured in several years, and it got skipped in the patching process. Owners of an ELBC2000 should be aware that their controller is still vulnerable, and there’s no patch available yet, as the vendor didn’t confirm that the ELBC2000 was vulnerable until the end of October, after it faced pressure from the researchers. ®

Critical Cisco remote code execution bug under attack
evening.text:
Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any authentication, according to warnings from the US government and security researchers.

CVE-2026-76466, which carries a 9.8 CVSS rating, affects Cisco Expressway-C and Cisco Expressway-E gateways configured in clusters, both virtual and physical appliances running vulnerable software. These provide firewall traversal, VPN-less remote access, and call routing for remote users connecting to voice, video, and messaging collaboration services.

The bug involves hard-coded authentication credentials and insufficient certificate validation in clustered Expressway deployments.

“An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands,” Cisco said in October, when it disclosed the bug and issued a software update that fixed the flaw. “A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device.”

At the time, the networking vendor said it wasn’t aware of any abuse of the vulnerability.

That all changed late last week, however, when Russian security firm F6 said it was investigating “the first observed case” of miscreants exploiting CVE-2026-76466, shortly after a public proof-of-concept exploit became available.

“The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices,” F6’s Cyber Defense Center said on Thursday. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.”

Specifically, the criminals prepared custom Python code to scan the victim’s network and identify files and folders shared over the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. The scripts were also designed to interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories for credentials and other sensitive information.

The Python scripts used in the attack indicated that the operator used an AI assistant, according to F6.

The security shop also noted that one of the key indicators of compromise is a nodeup “wombat@127.0.0.1” entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices.

A day later, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-76466 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and told federal agencies to patch by Monday.

Cisco updated its advisory on Monday to acknowledge CISA’s addition, while noting that it has no direct evidence of active exploitation. The Register reached out to the networking and security vendor for additional details about the scope of the attacks, but did not receive any response. We will update this story as we learn more. ®

evening.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
evening.text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well. 

Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm. 

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious). 

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.

“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models. 

The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “terrible” and “bizarre.” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”

It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing. 

Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines. If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.

Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.

But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.

Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

The Ancient Thracian heartland of Bulgaria says it has shut down a cyberespionage operation that gave intruders access to government networks for five years – the longest-running known campaign against its administration.

Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation said the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government institutions to exchange information in 2021.

"The incident was discovered thanks to the new national cybersecurity system, which for the first time provides a single picture of what is happening in state networks," the ministry added.

"Without it, this activity would most likely have remained hidden for an indefinite period of time."

Bulgaria acknowledged that "sensitive information related to the work of the state" was accessed, but did not specify the scale of the compromise.

Innovation and Digital Transformation Minister Ivan Vasilev said attackers had downloaded more than 130 GB of data over five years. He also put the volume at 62 million pages.

The Register contacted the Bulgarian government for confirmation of these numbers.

The ministry said that it has not yet found any evidence that citizens' personal data was compromised, and that the affected infrastructure "will be under increased surveillance for 90 days" in case the attackers try to regain access.

Vasilev said multiple international hacking groups had accessed government systems since 2021. He did not specify the names of these groups, however, nor did he name any specific countries that may have been involved.

In a follow-up interview with bTV, Vasilev blamed political instability and frequent changes of ministerial leadership for leaving government systems inadequately protected.

A representative of the Progressive Bulgaria party, which back in May won Bulgaria's eighth general election in five years, Vasilev said the "constant change of leadership" means "important things for the state do not actually happen."

Vasilev said the intrusion was discovered over the summer as the national cybersecurity system was upgraded, and that teams had spent the past three to four months removing the attackers. ®

evening.title: Satellite Imagery Suggests Russia May Be Deploying RS-28 Sarmat Missiles
evening.text:
Fresh satellite analysis from the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) indicates that Russia is moving forward with deploying its RS-28 Sarmat intercontinental ballistic missiles with the 62nd Missile Division near Uzhur in the Krasnoyarsk region, even though the program has struggled through years of delays, a September 2024 silo explosion, and a November 2025 launch crash.
Images captured in June 2026 show specialized transport vehicles, a crane, and an open launch silo signs that a missile section and potentially its payload are already underground, though analysts cannot yet verify if the system is on full combat alert. Built to replace aging Soviet-era hardware, the liquid-fueled Sarmat is designed to carry up to 15 nuclear warheads or hypersonic glide vehicles and could reach the United States via an unconventional southern polar flight path to complicate missile defense systems.
The apparent rollout coincides with renewed activity at a separate testing site in Dombarovsky and follows September 2026 SIPRI data showing Moscow’s deployed nuclear warhead count has risen for a fourth straight year to 1,796, its highest total in nine years.
Sarmat is a two-stage liquid-propelled ICBM with a post-boost phase vehicle and is intended to replace Russia’s RS-20V Voevoda (RS-SS-18 Satan Mod 5) and UR-100N (RS-SS-19 Stiletto Mod 4) ICBMs. Sarmat may carry up to 15 multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicles or potentially multiple hypersonic boost-glide vehicles.

evening.title: Microsoft mega outage: Report reveals testing gaps and emails that never arrived
evening.text:
Some emails never reached their recipients during November's Microsoft 365 outage, the company has confirmed in a final report that also exposes gaps in its testing and recovery procedures.

The post-incident report details how a Windows defect brought down Exchange Online and disrupted features across other Microsoft 365 services. For affected users, the cloud became someone else's unavailable computer.

A preliminary report had already blamed a July code change, combined with a failover and reduced capacity. The final report confirms those findings and sets out Microsoft's plans to improve change auditing and recovery procedures, and add spare capacity. The defect affected Microsoft's gateway server configuration, not standard Windows deployments.

The epic outage (named the "Microsoft long weekend" by some wags) kicked off on November 12 and wasn't fully resolved until November 14.

Microsoft extended its delivery retry window to 48 hours, but some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes inactive for more than 30 days still expired, generating non-delivery reports. The company said all queued enterprise messages were eventually delivered, with none found permanently lost.

The report is grim, particularly in how the failure ramped up as US users came online to find gateway servers toppling over. At the worst point, more than 80 percent of North American gateway servers were unresponsive.

The problem proved elusive, and it took Microsoft some time to identify the change and deploy a fix.

Microsoft has had a week to ponder what it did and did not do, and the report has some next steps to avoid a repeat of November's events. Some are obvious, and some are a little surprising.

Working to reduce the blast radius of failures is an obvious one, and actions include partitioning and isolation to ensure failures can be contained before taking down traffic globally. Recovery procedures also need improvement, along with communication and capacity to ensure there is sufficient headroom.

Microsoft's load tests used older, lower-core-count hardware, making them less likely to expose a defect that worsened on newer machines. The company now plans to test newer hardware with more realistic traffic and peak loads, and broaden its failover testing.

Microsoft also plans to improve diagnostics and change auditing so engineers can identify troublesome Windows changes faster. July's defect had been running worldwide for more than three months before it brought the gateways down. ®

evening.title: Pakistan’s J-35A Fighter Ambitions Continue, but Delivery Timeline Remains Uncertain
evening.text:
Rumours of Pakistan acquiring China’s J-35A stealth fighter have come up again, although some defence analyst believe the programme will not move forward as fast as it was previously reported. Although there have been multiple rumours of an impending induction in the past two years, there has yet to be an official announcement by China and Pakistan that a production contract has been signed or that the programme is in the delivery phase.
Latest evaluations suggest that Pakistan’s introduction of the fifth-generation fighter aircraft might be delayed by several years – three to four years according to some analysts, while others expect the delay to be a year or two more. Some suggest that it will take five or even six years before the first flight prototype enters PAF service. However, such assessments are best viewed as speculative.
The biggest driver identified by analysts is China’s own military modernisation effort. The Shenyang-built J-35A is among China’s latest stealth fighters, and its manufacturing capacity is likely to be largely directed towards servicing the demand of the PLAAF (People’s Liberation Army Air Force) and potentially the PLAN (People’s Liberation Army Navy), which is likely to fly the carrier-based versions of the aircraft.
At the same time, it is growing its fifth-generation combat fleet and developing new carriers to operate its stealth fighters. In such a scenario, analysts said Beijing might focus on its homeland demand before adopting a foreign-focused export strategy.
Another factor that contributes to the pessimistic outlook is the difference between a heavily promoted product and an aircraft that is ready for export. The J-35 has been heavily promoted at major Chinese defence shows and international airshows and there is a perception that the aircraft will be available for export within a short period. Defence analysts point out that appearances are not the same as sustaining series production for export markets.
And while fighter aircraft deliveries are the core. Massive Supply Chain, Engine Life Availability, Avionics fit, weapons validation and certification, long term logistics planning, etc. These present-day industrial realities tend to turn up the haphazard planning of public pronouncement, often pushing first export deliveries far off the public radar.
Of course, a strategic calculus is also at play. The sale of fifth-generation stealth technology would not only be a major international agreement, but one in which Beijing would need to weigh economic interests against preserving sensitive technology and regional security calculations. China has always been very cautious about exporting its most advanced military equipment, especially platforms that feature next-generation sensors, low-observable technologies and networking capabilities.
By Pakistan’s own accounts, the government has taken a more modest public stance concerning the sale. Pakistani officials have tended to pass up opportunities to validate the media reports of potential delivery dates or delayed induction dates, rather than verify the news of an official signed government-to-government agreement and specific timeline. This conservative approach has led to questions about the progress of negotiations and programme timetable.
In addition, the proposed deal is thought to be much wider than the fighter. Some articles have indicated that Pakistan is also looking at a broader military modernisation program with Chinese equipment, which includes the KJ-500 airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft and the HQ-19 long-range air and missile defence system. Bringing together a constellation of sophisticated systems would further complicate any requirement for financing, training, logistics, infrastructure and production schedules.
The J-35A represents a key goal for Pakistan’s air force. The aircraft is often seen as the foundation for Islamabad’s future drive to update and expand its combat aircraft inventory and enhance its capacity to operate in ever more contested airspace. A fifth-generation type offers stand-off radar stealth, sensor fusion, network-centric warfare, and beyond-visual-range combat advantages (if the export model maintains these).
The programme is also indicative of Pakistan’s deepening tilt towards Chinese defence hardware as Western procurement sources dry up. China has become Pakistan’s main supplier of weapons over the last two decades, helping procure everything from the JF-17 fighter, to HQ-9/P air defences, naval frigates and submarines and unmanned aerial vehicles.
However, there is still much uncertainty about the J-35A programme. A production contract, delivery schedule and number of aircraft procured have not been announced by either China or Pakistan. Most of the existing information on timelines is still based on media reports, analyst estimates or unofficial sources.

evening.title: No formal bilateral talks between India, Pak on sidelines of SCO forum
evening.text:
There were “no formal bilateral talks” held between India and Pakistan on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum, Union Culture Secretary Vivek Aggarwal said on Sunday. Pakistan’s Federal Minister Musadik Masood Malik attended the three-day forum here hosted by India at the historic Purana Quila.
Malik later in the evening, interacting with the media, said, “When you will call me for talk on Indus (Water Treaty), that time, we will surely talk on Indus (treaty). This time, you have not called me here for (talks on) the Indus treaty; this time you have called me to talk…,” Malik said.
“You have called me this time to talk about the issue in the context of the SCO forum, the regional issues, its relationship with culture, for which I am here,” he told reporters here.
The forum was hosted by the Ministry of Culture and the Ministry of External Affairs.
Earlier, at a press interaction held at the venue, shortly before the closure of the forum asked if any formal bilateral talks were held between India and Pakistan on the sidelines; Aggarwal said, “There were no formal bilateral talks between the two sides.” However, he said that members of the Indian side did have interactions with him over banquets and during the conference, as well as there were other “informal discussions” with him during the course of the forum, as with other ministers too.
“In general, there were also meetings between ministers and heads of delegations, as the aim of this (multilateral) forum is to exchange views, so there were many meetings, and a lot of things were discussed,” the culture secretary said.
However, he didn’t specify how many bilateral talks took place during the course of the Forum hosted by India from November 20-22.
Asked if any bilateral meeting took place with Iran, he said, “There was a bilateral meeting with Iran. And India is in constant touch with Iran, and on areas in which there can be any cultural exchange, we are always in discussion. And discussions took place during the Summit too.” The secretary said that during the bilateral meeting, “ideas have been thrown, though no such project has been concretised yet. But the discussions and engagements are on”.
The Iranian Embassy in India, in a post on X on Sunday, said that, at the civilisational summit, Tehran proposed setting up an “SCO Joint Network for Written Heritage and Civilisational Memory”.
Dr Faridoddin Faridasr, Cultural Counsellor of the Islamic Republic of Iran in India, addressed the First SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi, highlighting the importance of shared civilisational heritage as a foundation for cultural cooperation and mutual understanding among SCO member states, it said.
In his remarks, he emphasised the historical role of the “Persian language as a language of science, literature, administration and cultural exchange across Central Asia, the Indian subcontinent and neighbouring regions, describing it as an important part of the shared cultural and historical heritage of the region”.
Referring to Iran’s successful cultural cooperation with India, he highlighted the activities of the Noor International Microfilm Centre, affiliated with the Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in New Delhi. Since 1990, the Centre has collaborated with 72 academic and cultural institutions in India, resulting in the digitisation of “more than 150,000 Persian and Arabic manuscripts,” the restoration and preservation of over three million pages of historical documents, and the preparation of nearly 300 catalogues, the embassy said.
Faridasr also referred to the ongoing joint projects with cultural institutions in Telangana and Hyderabad for the digitisation, restoration and preservation of historical Persian documents and manuscripts.
As a practical initiative to strengthen regional cultural cooperation, he proposed the establishment of an “SCO Joint Network for Written Heritage and Civilizational Memory.” “The proposed network would focus on the preservation and digitisation of manuscripts and historical documents, the exchange of technical expertise and training in manuscript restoration, and the promotion of shared linguistic and literary heritage through joint research, publications and exhibitions,” the embassy said in a detailed post on X.
He reaffirmed Iran’s “readiness to share its experience and technical expertise with other SCO member states”, stressing that the preservation of shared civilisational heritage provides an important opportunity to strengthen mutual trust, cultural understanding and cooperation across the region.
The forum was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on November 20. It saw the participation of delegates from various Shanghai Cooperation Organisation member countries, including Pakistan and other countries.

evening.title: India’s ties with Russia can help push for end to Ukraine war: Dutch FM
evening.text:
The Netherlands views India’s continued engagement with Russia as an “added value,” as New Delhi can use its ties with Moscow to persuade it to end the war in Ukraine, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said.
Berendsen is on an official visit to India from November 22 to 23. He co-chaired the inaugural Foreign Ministers’ Meeting with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar in New Delhi on Sunday and reviewed the India-Netherlands Strategic Partnership.
“We understand that India has its own history, its own role in the world and its own relations,” Berendsen told PTI on Sunday, responding to a question on India’s strategic autonomy and its continued engagement with Moscow.
“We actually see it as an added value of our relationship with India that it has a relationship with Russia and can also use that relationship to show Russia that it needs to put an end to this war and accept a ceasefire,” he said.
The Russia-Ukraine war, in its fifth year, continues with intensified attacks from both sides. Russia has stepped up strikes on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, while US-brokered peace talks have made little progress beyond a prisoner swap. Berendsen said India and the Netherlands, as trading countries, shared concerns over maritime security and freedom of navigation, and needed to work together to address challenges in an increasingly uncertain world.
“I think we’re dealing with the same challenges: how to decrease dependencies, how to be more strategically autonomous on critical raw materials, technology and energy,” he said.
“If you want to do that, you need to diversify, which means new partnerships. I think the Netherlands, the EU and India are doing exactly that,” he added.
On trade, he described the proposed India-European Union free trade agreement, expected to be signed in December, as a crucial step that could open opportunities beyond merchandise trade.
Berendsen also welcomed the memorandum of understanding (MoU) between Tata Electronics and Dutch semiconductor major ASML, saying cooperation in the semiconductor ecosystem offered significant possibilities for both countries.
The MoU was signed in May during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to the Netherlands to support India’s first commercial 300 mm (12-inch) semiconductor fabrication plant in Dholera, Gujarat.
“…it is not only about signing a document; it is the starting point of strengthening the partnership, so we are taking the next steps,” Berendsen told reporters at a press conference after his meeting with Jaishankar.
Berendsen said his meeting with Jaishankar was their sixth this year, reflecting the growing engagement between the two countries. He said cooperation was being strengthened in sectors such as energy, security, technology, water management and agriculture.
Jaishankar and his Dutch counterpart on Sunday discussed the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and the situation in the Black Sea, with Berendsen appreciating India’s efforts towards facilitating a possible arrangement for safe passage of grain shipments through the region.
The remarks come amid increasing attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea during the Russia-Ukraine war.
Berendsen said the war had affected global food security and the Netherlands valued India’s role in working towards a solution.
In his opening remarks at the meeting, Jaishankar said the two sides had elevated their relationship to a Strategic Partnership and were looking to expand cooperation in areas including semiconductors, technology, defence and renewable energy, while continuing their traditional collaboration in water, agriculture and health.
“There are shared challenges. I think terrorism is one, climate change is another, where it’s important we work together. So I’m really pleased today to have this chance to co-chair our inaugural dialogue mechanism for reviewing the strategic partnership,” Jaishankar said.
Berendsen is scheduled to meet Electronics and Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw on Monday before departing from India.

The Sukhoi design bureau in Russia is reportedly working on an adaptation of a heavy air-to-surface (or anti-ship) missile for the Su-30 fighter, on behalf of an unnamed customer. That could well be the basis of a new export opportunity for the air-launched BrahMos supersonic cruise missile.
Oleg Pankov, head of design at Sukhoi, confirmed the development in an interview with Russia’s Zvezda TV channel (via TASS on 23 November). He said that a customer requirement had arisen to equip the aircraft with a heavy air-to-surface or air-to-ship missile, that design work was in progress and that the only thing required would be minor modifications to the airframe.
“There is a study, there is a desire and we just need some minor structural tweaks. It’s entirely realistic,” Pankov said.
Neither the customer nor the missile in question was identified. The announcement is of course of some interest as the Indian Air Force’s Su-30MKI is the only Su-30 currently in operational service carrying the air-launched Brahmos-A. It is therefore entirely possible that a foreign Su-30 operator could be interested in such a capability.
The BrahMos-A integration was a significant engineering exercise. The 2.5 tonne missile necessitated modification to the Su-30MKI airframe (in particular the strengthening of the airframe around the fuselage attachment points), as well as mechanical, electrical and software changes. The aircraft itself also went through a lot of aerodynamic and missile separation work.
Hindustan Aeronautics eventually did the modification work themselves using their own design capability. The first Su-30MKI modified for BrahMos integration was handed over to BrahMos Aerospace in February 2015. Brahmos described it as an indigenous engineering solution with the design work having been carried out by HAL’s own design team.
The programme had earlier run into issues over the cost of Russian assistance. A 2011 report indicated that Russia had requested additional payment to redesign and strengthen the Su-30 for air launch. The Indian authorities then looked at the possibility of HAL doing the work at home rather than accept the additional cost that had been proposed.
Pankov’s most recent comments might well be indicative of another Su-30 operator looking at a heavy missile option. There are a number of countries who operate the export versions of the aircraft (Malaysia and Vietnam to name but two). Both of those countries could in theory be interested in a long range anti-ship capability, particularly in the context of their maritime security. There is of course no public indication as to which of those countries (if any) is the customer that Sukhoi has in mind.
Indonesia is another country to keep an eye on. They have Su-30s and have been linked to a BrahMos acquisition. Reuters in July 2026 reported that Indonesia was to acquire BrahMos as part of a wider defence package. That report was specifically about the missile acquisition and doesn’t in any way establish a requirement for the air-launched version or for any modification to the Indonesian Su-30s.
The difference is that integrating the BrahMos-A isn’t just a case of bolting a missile onto another aircraft. You have to look at the Su-30’s airframe configuration, the launcher arrangement, the electrical interfaces, the software and the safe separation characteristics for each variant. The modifications made to the Indian Su-30MKI cannot be simply carried over to other Su-30 variants.
For BrahMos Aerospace a foreign air-launched customer would be a significant extension of the missile beyond its current IAF application. It would also be a demonstration of the potential of the India-Russia JV’s technology on a foreign platform that the customer would already be operating (i.e. the Su-30).

Las Vegas welcomed Formula 1 to its streets this past weekend. And for the first time since the event’s inception in 2023, the Grand Prix delivered on a long-promised spectacle. The racing was closer to an IndyCar oval race than anything F1 fans will have seen since slipstreaming was the order of the day at places like Monza and Hockenheim, back when humans were still landing on the Moon and downforce had yet to fundamentally change racing.

The Vegas street circuit—the one that looks like an upside-down pig—is an extreme outlier on the calendar. It has plenty of long straights, so this year’s cars still suffer from energy starvation throughout the lap, as the inadequate size of their lithium-ion hybrid batteries means they become depleted very quickly, leaving the cars on just over half power with their V6 engines operating without the benefit of the hybrid’s electric motor.

But the 17 turns are mostly all low speed, so there’s no risk of seeing the cars driving demoralizingly slowly through corners that are supposed to test one’s mettle.

evening.title: IG Defence Successfully Test-Fires JWALA MK-1 Autonomous Counter-Drone Missile at Pokhran
evening.text:
In a landmark development for India’s indigenous defence industry, IG Defence has successfully test-fired JWALA MK-1 at Pokhran, Rajasthan. The company describes it as India’s first autonomous Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (CUAS) Micro-Missile System, marking a significant milestone in the development of next-generation indigenous counter-drone technologies.
With an operational range of up to 5 kilometres, JWALA MK-1 has been developed as an indigenous, autonomous and cost-effective solution to address the rapidly evolving threat posed by hostile unmanned aerial systems.
The proliferation of unmanned aerial systems is fundamentally transforming modern military operations. Recent international conflicts, including the US-Iran confrontation, have highlighted the growing deployment of relatively inexpensive attack drones and the economic challenges of countering them using high-cost conventional air-defence interceptors.
This emerging battlefield reality has exposed a critical cost imbalance: low-cost aerial threats can compel militaries to deploy significantly more expensive interception systems, placing pressure on interceptor inventories, ammunition sustainability and the economics of modern warfare.For India, with its complex security environment and evolving aerial threats, developing affordable, scalable and indigenous counter-UAS technologies is a strategic necessity.
JWALA MK-1 has been developed as an integrated autonomous counter-drone micro-missile system with a stated operational range of 5 kilometres. According to IG Defence, the system is designed to identify potential hostile drone targets, classify them and facilitate their airborne neutralisation through an integrated mission autonomy architecture.
A defining feature of JWALA MK-1 is its integration with GRID, IG Defence’s proprietary AI-powered Mission Autonomy and Battle Management System, which acts as the intelligence backbone coordinating the system’s operational kill chain.
GRID brings together sensor integration, target detection, identification, classification, mission decision-making and engagement management within a unified architecture, enabling coordinated mission execution. Speaking about the development, Bodhisattwa Sanghapriya, Founder and CEO of IG Defence, said: “GRID is not just a standalone Mission Autonomy and Battle Management System; it is the intelligence backbone managing the entire kill chain of JWALA MK-1. From sensor integrat
ion and target detection to identification, classification, mission decision-making and engagement management, GRID’s AI-driven orchestration brings the entire operational chain together within a unified architecture.
Our vision is to build indigenous defence systems where hardware and software are developed together, with autonomy and intelligence at their core. India must not simply manufacture weapons; we must build the intelligence, technology and integrated systems that power the future battlefield. That is the capability we are building at IG Defence.”
Commenting on the operational significance of the development, Wing Commander Anoop Sharma, Associate Vice President, IG Defence, said: “The character of warfare is evolving rapidly, and the growing proliferation of unmanned aerial threats demands a new approach to air defence. Countering low-cost drones with expensive conventional systems is a challenge that modern militaries can no longer overlook. India needs indigenous, reliable and cost-effective solutions that can address these emerging threats at scale.
JWALA MK-1 represents an important step in that direction. Our focus is on developing an integrated counter-drone capability that combines advanced technology, mission autonomy and operational effectiveness. Such indigenous systems are essential for strengthening India’s preparedness for future battlefield challenges and advancing our defence self-reliance.”
The successful test at Pokhran marks another milestone in India’s expanding private defence manufacturing ecosystem. As the country accelerates its defence indigenisation efforts, indigenous missile technologies, autonomous systems and AI-powered battle management platforms will play an increasingly important role in strengthening national security.
JWALA MK-1 reflects IG Defence’s ambition to move beyond conventional defence manufacturing towards developing integrated, intelligent and indigenous defence capabilities. By bringing together micro-missile technology, autonomous mission management and proprietary AI-powered battle management, the company aims to contribute to India’s next generation of counter-drone solutions.The achievement reinforces a larger national objective: reducing critical defence import dependencies, strengthening indigenous technological capabilities and building a self-reliant Indian defence ecosystem.
India must not merely prepare for the future of warfare. India must build the technologies that will define it.
